text: Real datasets have gaps: a skipped form field, a dropped sensor reading, a join that found no match. Most scikit-learn models error out the moment they see a NaN. The real question isn't just how to fill it, but where. Done inside a pipeline, imputation stays repeatable and leak-free.

Look before you fill. On fifteen hundred illustrative customers, about eighteen percent of monthly charges are missing, and those missing rows churn at fifty-seven percent, versus twenty-five percent for everyone else. The gap itself carries signal. Dropping every row with a gap would also throw away four hundred twenty-three of those fifteen hundred customers.

The rule for imputing is the same as for scaling: learn fill values from training data only. Put SimpleImputer inside a ColumnTransformer, nested in a Pipeline, and every cross-validation fold learns its own median from its own training rows, never peeking at the rows it will be tested on.

Compare three strategies with five-fold cross-validation on ROC AUC. Plain median imputation scores point seven six oh. A KNN imputer with five neighbors scores the same, point seven six oh. Median imputation plus a missing-value indicator jumps to point seven nine eight.

That jump matters more than the imputer itself. add_indicator equals True appends a zero-one column flagging which rows were originally missing, and the model can now see that flag directly. It is recovering the same churn signal we found by hand: missingness itself was informative.

Two more options. Dropping rows with gaps looks tempting, but it scored point seven nine six on only one thousand seventy-seven surviving rows, a different, easier test set, not a fair comparison. And HistGradientBoostingClassifier accepts NaN directly, learning a best split direction for missing values; it scored point seven six one with no imputation at all.

Measure missingness first, ask whether missing itself means something, impute inside the pipeline, and try an indicator column before assuming a fancier imputer will help. Next: three applied walkthroughs, starting with churn prediction.
